item.title: Your Tool Schema Has One Field That Controls Whether Claude Calls the Right Function — and It's Not the Name
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: The description field is a mini-prompt — write when to call, when not to, what the side effect is, and what comes back. Most tool schemas get the name right and stop there.
item.content:encoded:
**The `description` field is a mini-prompt — write when to call, when not to, what the side effect is, and what comes back. Most tool schemas get the name right and stop there.**
Claude decides whether to call a tool — and how to fill in its arguments — from three things: the tool name, the `description` field, and the `input_schema`. Most schemas get the name right and stop there. The description is where most agents go wrong.
**What the description field is actually for.** It's not a label. It's the instruction Claude reads before every tool call to decide whether this is the right tool and what it will receive. A one-sentence description that restates the name ("search orders in the database") tells Claude nothing it doesn't already know. An effective description answers four questions:
1. **When should I call this?** ("Call when the user asks about an existing order or order status") 2. **When should I NOT call this?** ("Not for creating new orders — use `create_order` for that") 3. **What is the side effect?** (for writes: "Cancels the order and triggers a refund if payment was collected") 4. **What does the response contain?** ("Returns order_id, status, items[], and shipping_address")
**Before:** ```python { "name": "search_orders", "description": "Search orders in the database.", ... } ```
**After:** ```python { "name": "search_orders", "description": ( "Look up one or more orders by order_id, customer_email, or date range. " "Use this when the user asks about an existing order — its status, items, or shipping. " "Do NOT use this to create or modify orders. " "Returns: order_id, status (pending|processing|shipped|delivered|cancelled), " "items[], shipping_address, and created_at." ), ... } ```
**The input_schema matters too.** Use `enum` for constrained fields — Claude picks the right value instead of guessing a string. Add a `description` on every property, especially when the parameter name is ambiguous. Mark `required` honestly — don't list optional parameters as required and then null-check in your code.
```python "properties": { "status_filter": { "type": "string", "enum": ["pending", "processing", "shipped", "delivered", "cancelled"], "description": "Only return orders in this status. Omit to return all statuses." } } ```
**The real limit.** When a tool list grows past 10–15 entries, Claude's selection accuracy drops even with good descriptions — the context becomes a long scan rather than a targeted lookup. If you hit this, narrow the available set with `tool_choice`, or decompose the agent so each subagent holds only the tools it actually needs.
**Sources:** [Designing Claude Connector Tools — sunpeak.ai](https://sunpeak.ai/blogs/claude-connector-tool-design/) · [Tool use best practices — docs.anthropic.com](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/tool-use/best-practices-for-tool-definitions)

item.title: Your LLM App Has No Regression Tests — DeepEval 4 Adds Pytest-Style Quality Gates in 20 Lines
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: DeepEval 4 lets you write LLM test cases like pytest fixtures and run them in CI: if output quality drops below a threshold, the build fails. @observe traces individual agent spans.
item.content:encoded:
**DeepEval 4 lets you write LLM test cases like pytest fixtures and run them in CI: if output quality drops below a threshold, the build fails.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Write test cases for your LLM app that run in CI and block a deploy when answer quality drops, retrieval fails to return relevant chunks, or an agent calls the wrong tool.
- `LLMTestCase` wraps one input/output pair and its retrieval context — the unit of every test - `deepeval test run` is the CI command (not `pytest`) — it runs DeepEval's own runner, which aggregates scores and handles async; `pytest` works but skips DeepEval's runner behavior - `@observe` on agent functions traces individual spans, letting you attach metrics at the retrieval step or tool-call step rather than only the final answer
**Walk-through.**
```bash pip install deepeval ```
```python # test_qa.py from deepeval import assert_test from deepeval.test_case import LLMTestCase from deepeval.metrics import AnswerRelevancyMetric, FaithfulnessMetric
def test_order_status_answer(): tc = LLMTestCase( input="What is the status of order #8821?", actual_output=run_my_agent("What is the status of order #8821?"), expected_output="Order #8821 is shipped.", retrieval_context=[ "Order #8821 — Status: shipped — Updated: 2026-09-06" ] ) assert_test(tc, [ AnswerRelevancyMetric(threshold=0.7), FaithfulnessMetric(threshold=0.8), ]) ```
```bash deepeval test run test_qa.py ```
Add `deepeval test run` to your CI step as a normal build stage — it exits non-zero when a test case fails, blocking the deploy.
**For agents, trace individual spans with `@observe`:**
```python from deepeval.tracing import observe
@observe() def retrieve_context(query: str) -> list[str]: return vector_db.search(query, top_k=5) ```
This turns each function call into a span in DeepEval's trace. You can attach metrics directly to the span rather than only the final output — useful for catching a retrieval step that returns stale documents even when the final answer looks plausible.
**Where this breaks down.** The default threshold of 0.5 is a starting value, not a quality guarantee — calibrate it on a labeled sample of your own data before making it a CI gate. DeepEval uses an LLM judge internally, which means eval itself costs tokens and isn't deterministic across runs; set a cheap judge model for CI speed. The cloud dashboard (Confident AI) is a paid service; local `deepeval test run` is free. These tests run offline against a fixed dataset — they don't monitor production traffic.
**Sources:** [DeepEval AI Agent Evaluation Quickstart — deepeval.com](https://deepeval.com/docs/getting-started-agents) · [DeepEval 4 tutorial for pytest-style LLM, RAG, and agent testing — qaskills.sh](https://qaskills.sh/blog/deepeval-llm-testing-guide) · [DeepEval alternatives compared — Braintrust](https://www.braintrust.dev/articles/deepeval-alternatives-2026)

item.title: One Task Per Claude Code Session — and How to Resume It the Next Day
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: --continue loads the most recent session for your directory; --resume picks an older one by ID. One task per session plus a short handoff note keeps multi-day coding work coherent.
item.content:encoded:
**`-c` and `-r` are the two flags that turn Claude Code into a persistent coding partner across days — but the flag alone isn't enough; one task per session and a short handoff note are what keep the work coherent.**
Claude Code saves every session automatically. The session ID, conversation history, and tool call results all persist to disk, scoped to the directory you were working in. Two flags get you back:
```bash # Resume the most recent session for this directory claude -c # short for --continue
# Pick from a list of older sessions for this directory claude -r # short for --resume; shows an interactive picker # Or pass a specific session ID (from claude sessions list) claude --resume "$session_id" ```
**When to use which.** Use `-c` for everyday continuity: you stopped mid-task last night, open a terminal this morning, and `claude -c` picks up exactly where you were. Use `-r` when you're juggling two parallel workstreams in the same project — a feature branch and a hotfix, for example — and you want to switch between them rather than starting fresh each time.
**One task per session.** The strongest pattern is: one session = one task. A session that did ten things becomes hard to resume coherently because the context mixes unrelated history. When a task finishes, let the session close and start a new one for the next thing. Use `-c` to continue the same task across a break, not to pile new tasks onto an old session.
**The handoff note.** When you stop mid-task, type a short status note before you exit:
``` /status: Refactoring the auth module — completed UserService, next is TokenStore. Tests pass. Stopped before wiring TokenStore into the middleware chain. ```
When you resume, Claude reads this and picks up without the re-orientation questions. Even three sentences of "where I stopped and what's next" cuts the warm-up time significantly.
**Limits to know.** Session context includes conversation history and tool results, but not your git working tree — always commit (or at least stash) before ending a session if you want the code state preserved separately from Claude's memory of it. For long tasks that span many sessions, context eventually grows large enough to need `/compact` — a summary step that compresses prior history so you keep working without hitting the context ceiling.
**Sources:** [Manage sessions — code.claude.com/docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions) · [Claude Code session management — SSD Nodes](https://www.ssdnodes.com/learn/claude-code-resume-and-session-history) · [Multi-session workflows — Claude Code Handbook](https://joeyyu23.github.io/claude-code-handbook/en/book2-advanced/18-multi-session)

item.title: Your RAG Answers Are Unverifiable Without This — Add Inline Citations in 20 Lines With LlamaIndex
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: LlamaIndex's CitationQueryEngine adds inline source citations to RAG answers — the difference between "here's an answer" and "here's an answer with the exact sentences it came from."
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Build a RAG pipeline where every answer cites the exact source chunks it drew from - Configure citation granularity — how many sentences per citation node, how the model attributes claims - Decide when citations add real value vs. when they add noise and latency
## Why citations matter
A plain RAG answer says "the refund window is 30 days." A cited answer says "the refund window is 30 days [Source 1: refund-policy.pdf, p. 2]." The first is useful; the second is auditable. Any production RAG system where the user needs to verify the answer — support knowledge bases, legal research, internal policy lookups — should be returning attributed answers.
LlamaIndex's `CitationQueryEngine` handles attribution automatically. It splits retrieved chunks into citation nodes and instructs the model to cite them inline.
## Setup
```bash pip install llama-index llama-index-llms-anthropic llama-index-embeddings-huggingface ```
## The 20-line pipeline
```python from llama_index.core import VectorStoreIndex, SimpleDirectoryReader from llama_index.core.query_engine import CitationQueryEngine
# Load and index your documents (swap in your vector store of choice) documents = SimpleDirectoryReader("./docs").load_data() index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(documents)
# Wrap with citation engine query_engine = CitationQueryEngine.from_args( index, similarity_top_k=5, # how many chunks to retrieve citation_chunk_size=512, # characters per citation node (default 512) )
response = query_engine.query("What is the refund policy for enterprise plans?")
# The response includes both the answer and source nodes print(response.response) # answer with inline [Source N] markers for i, node in enumerate(response.source_nodes): print(f"\nSource {i+1}:") print(node.node.text[:300]) # the cited passage print(f"Score: {node.score:.3f}") ```
## What the output looks like
``` The enterprise refund policy allows cancellation within 30 days [Source 1]. Refunds are prorated for annual plans [Source 2]. Custom contracts may have different terms as negotiated [Source 3].
Source 1: (from enterprise-terms.pdf) "Enterprise customers may cancel within 30 days of the billing date for a full refund..." ```
## Limits to know
**Longer, slower responses.** The citation node splitting and inline attribution add tokens to both the prompt and the completion. On a 5-chunk retrieval, expect 20-40% more output tokens compared to a plain query engine. Benchmark this against your latency and cost requirements before shipping to production.
**Chunk size affects citation quality.** Very small chunks (under 200 characters) produce unhelpful micro-citations. Very large chunks (over 1,000 characters) make it hard for the model to attribute precisely. The default 512-character window is a reasonable starting point; tune it against your document structure.
**Not a replacement for retrieval quality.** `CitationQueryEngine` attributes whatever was retrieved — if the retriever pulled the wrong chunks, the citations will be confidently wrong. Fix retrieval quality first, then add attribution.
**Sources:** [Build RAG with inline citations — LlamaIndex docs](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/python/examples/workflow/citation_query_engine/) · [RAG with citations — Zilliz blog](https://zilliz.com/blog/retrieval-augmented-generation-with-citations) · [LLM source citation with LangChain — ReadyTensor](https://app.readytensor.ai/publications/llm-source-citation-with-langchain-dXocR7whrOTR) · [LlamaIndex examples — Real Python](https://realpython.com/llamaindex-examples/)

item.title: Copilot's Content Exclusion Policies Weren't Applying to Agentic Tasks Until September 2
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: GitHub Copilot content exclusions now apply to the Copilot app and CLI. If excluded files were in your agentic task context before September 2, they no longer are.
item.content:encoded:
**If your org has content exclusion policies configured in GitHub Copilot, those policies were not being enforced in the Copilot app or Copilot CLI — agentic tasks were outside the policy's scope until September 2.**
GitHub's content exclusion feature lets enterprise, organization, and repository admins define which files Copilot cannot use as context — secrets, regulated data, proprietary logic. These policies worked in the IDE chat and completions. They did not apply when the Copilot app or Copilot CLI ran multi-step tasks. Excluded files could and did appear in the agent's working context.
The change (shipped September 2) closes that gap. Copilot now respects exclusion policies uniformly across IDE, app, and CLI.
**What to check now.** If your organization uses Copilot Business or Enterprise and has exclusion rules configured, audit whether those glob patterns actually cover what you intended. A few post-fix reviews have found that patterns written for IDE file paths (e.g., `**/secrets/**`) didn't match the path formats the CLI was passing before enforcement started — the exclusion rules were there, but the patterns had silent gaps.
**Limit:** Content exclusion is a Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise feature. Individual Copilot Free and Pro users cannot configure exclusion policies.
**Why it matters:** If you were relying on content exclusion to keep credentials, private configs, or IP out of AI context during agentic runs, you now have actual enforcement — not just IDE-level enforcement. Verify your patterns hold before assuming the coverage is complete.
**Sources:** [Content exclusions GA in Copilot app and CLI — GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-09-02-content-exclusions-generally-available-in-copilot-app-and-cli/) · [Copilot content exclusion gap analysis — devactivity.com](https://devactivity.com/posts/apps-tools/github-copilot-s-content-exclusion-a-critical-blind-spot-for-agentic-workflows/) · [Quest Review Center coverage](https://questreviewcenter.com/software-reviews/github-enhances-copilot-content-exclusion-amidst-complex-remote-and-linked-file-challenges/)

item.title: Your Subagent System Prompt Breaks When It's Too Long for the CLI — Pass It From a File
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code v2.1.261 adds --append-subagent-system-prompt-file so you can load a subagent system prompt from a file — fixing CLI length limits and escaping failures for complex agent contexts.
item.content:encoded:
**Pass your subagent system prompt as a file path instead of a CLI argument — `--append-subagent-system-prompt-file` ships in Claude Code v2.1.261 and removes the length and escaping ceiling on complex agent contexts.**
When you run Claude Code in CI or as a scheduled task with multi-step agents, you eventually hit a ceiling: the subagent system prompt lives on the command line, and shell argument length limits — plus escaping of quotes, newlines, and special characters — make large prompts fragile and hard to maintain. A 2,000-word researcher context that works fine in a shell heredoc starts misfiring when it has to survive `JSON.stringify` → CLI arg → shell re-parsing.
`--append-subagent-system-prompt-file` reads the subagent system prompt from a file and appends it to the default context:
```bash claude \ --append-subagent-system-prompt-file ./prompts/researcher-agent.md \ --permission-prompts none \ "Summarize this week's AI research and flag anything security-relevant" ```
The file contents are appended to (not a replacement for) the built-in subagent context, so the agent still carries standard Claude Code behaviors — only your additions live in the file.
**Practical uses:** - CI pipelines that spawn agents with domain-specific rules (coding standards, output schemas, which repos are in scope) - Scheduled tasks where the agent context changes per-run without a code change — update the file, not the workflow YAML - Keeping sensitive-but-not-secret context (internal service names, team conventions) out of command history
**The limit to know:** the file is read once at session start, not spawned fresh per subagent. If your workflow fans out to subagents that need different contexts, you still need the Agent SDK's programmatic `system` parameter — this flag is for the common case where one prompt governs all subagents in a session.
**Sources:** [Claude Code v2.1.261 release notes — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog) · [v2.1.261 changelog summary — dev.classmethod.jp](https://dev.classmethod.jp/en/articles/20260905-cc-updates-v2-1-261/) · [Release v2.1.261 — github.com/anthropics/claude-code](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/releases/tag/v2.1.261)

item.title: Import Your Design System Into Claude Design Before Writing the First Prompt
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Design's design-system import (shipped June 2026) pulls in your tokens and components from GitHub, Figma, or tokens JSON so every generated screen starts from your system, not generic HTML defaults.
item.content:encoded:
**Before the June 2026 update, every Claude Design screen started from generic HTML defaults. The design-system import changes the starting point: your tokens, your components, your variants — no substitution pass after export.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Generate screens in Claude Design that open with your real button variants, type scale, and spacing tokens already applied — meaning the first thing you review is layout and content, not a round of find-and-replace on `bg-blue-500`.
**Three things to know going in:** - Claude Design accepts design systems from three sources: a connected GitHub repo (reads your CSS variables or Tailwind config), a Figma file export (tokens + component JSON), or a raw upload (design tokens JSON, Storybook config) - Once imported, generated screens reference your token names, not generic values — if your system defines `--color-action-primary`, that's what appears in the output - The import is a snapshot, not a live sync — update it when your design system changes, or generated output will drift toward stale values
**How to set it up (four steps):**
1. Open Claude Design → Settings → Design System → Import 2. Choose your source: GitHub repo URL (Claude Design clones and parses it), Figma export zip, or tokens JSON upload 3. Review the parse report — Claude Design lists which tokens and component variants it recognized; fix any misses before you start designing (typically spacing and motion tokens need the most cleanup) 4. Start a new session; the component selector now surfaces your variants, and generated screens reference your token names from the first output
**What it doesn't import:** Interaction states (hover, focus, error), animation specs, and semantic usage rules ("use action-primary for CTAs, not brand-primary") don't survive the import. Those still belong in your DESIGN.md or explicit prompts — Claude Design reads token values, not intent. If you skip this, generated screens will use your token names but often pick the wrong one for the context.

item.title: Three Fable 5.1 API Changes Your Existing Integrations Need to Test Against Now
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Fable 5.1 (Sept 1) ships three API-level breaking changes around thinking blocks and conversation editing — and one change that silently drops thinking output rather than erroring.
item.content:encoded:
**Fable 5.1 launched September 1 with three API-level breaking changes. The most dangerous one doesn't error — it silently drops thinking blocks when conversation history is edited before them.**
Anthropic shipped [Claude Fable 5.1](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/release-notes/overview) with changes that don't appear in the model's output quality — they change what the API accepts:
1. **Thinking block constraint.** Editing anything before a Fable 5.1 thinking block (system prompt, tools array, an earlier message) causes the next request to error or silently drop the block — per [the migration guide](https://blog.4sapi.com/blog/claude-fable-5-1-migration-guide), which variant depends on how the account was provisioned. 2. **Conversation editing restriction.** For API accounts created on or after September 1, manually editing Claude's prior context while preserving a thinking block transcript is no longer permitted. 3. **Cache read price drop.** Cache reads fall from $1 to $0.25 per million tokens (per Anthropic's release notes) — this one you likely want.
**Why it matters:** Any multi-turn pipeline that patches conversation history, hot-swaps system prompts mid-session, or injects tool results around thinking blocks needs an explicit compatibility test before migrating from Fable 5. The silent-drop behavior is the specific failure mode to check: your pipeline continues running, your logs show no error, and your reasoning output is gone.

item.title: Use the Exploration Phase — Three Design Directions Before You Commit, Then Write the Brief That Drives Implementation
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Before committing to a layout, ask Claude Design for three explicit directions in one prompt, compare them structurally, pick the least wrong, and write a decision brief that Claude Code can implement without re-interpreting the design.
item.content:encoded:
**Ask for three explicit layout directions in one prompt, pick the least wrong, and write a decision brief that Claude Code can implement without re-interpreting the design.**
Most teams use Claude Design to generate one screen and then iterate on it. That works for refinement, but it locks you into the first interpretation of the problem before you have seen any alternatives.
A more useful starting move: ask for three explicitly different directions in a single prompt.
``` Generate three layout directions for the admin dashboard header: - Direction A: compact, content-first, no sidebar (mobile-first) - Direction B: sidebar navigation with persistent page context, desktop-optimized - Direction C: command-bar style, keyboard-driven, minimal visual chrome
Use our existing Header, Sidebar, and CommandBar component names where they fit. ```
Claude Design produces all three in one turn. What you are comparing is not aesthetics — it is structural decisions: which direction solves the navigation problem the way your users will actually encounter it, and which fits your existing component tree without major surgery.
Once you pick a direction, do not iterate on it in Claude Design with vague feedback like "make it less busy." Write a decision brief instead:
``` Going with Direction B. Adjustments before implementation: - Use 16px gap between sidebar items instead of the generated 24px - Replace the custom header with our existing <AppShell> component - The card grid in the main panel can use <DataCard> from our library as-is ```
Hand that brief to Claude Code as context. It becomes the spec — grounded in your actual component names, not in generic HTML the design tool guessed at.
**The limits.** Claude Design generates all three directions from the same prompt, so they share the same interpretation of your design system. If you want directions that disagree on the *problem* — not just the *layout* — you need separate sessions with explicitly different framing.
The other limit is that Claude Design's component names in the exploration output are still guesses. The brief above is doing real work by replacing "Card" with `<DataCard>` — that substitution is what keeps Claude Code inside your design system rather than building its own.

item.title: Change Effort Mid-Conversation Without Busting the Cache — Per-Message Effort on Fable 5.1
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: On Fable 5.1, Mythos 5.1, and Opus 5, inject a role:system message with the new effort level to change it mid-conversation without invalidating the cached prefix — useful for sessions that need high effort for planning and low effort for follow-up turns.
item.content:encoded:
**Inject a `role:system` message with the new effort level to step down mid-conversation on Fable 5.1, Mythos 5.1, and Opus 5 (beta) — the cached prefix stays intact.**
Long agentic sessions often need two effort modes: `high` for the initial analysis or planning turn, `low` for the follow-up turns (summarize, format, confirm). The naive fix — change `output_config.effort` at the top level on the next request — starts a new cache prefix. Every token you have already paid for gets re-billed.
Per-message effort (beta header: `mid-conversation-output-config-2026-07-01`) gives you a cleaner path. Add a system message with empty `content` and the new effort level in `output_config.effort`. The new level takes effect from the next user turn forward; the cached prefix before that message is unchanged.
```python response = client.beta.messages.create( model="claude-fable-5-1", max_tokens=8096, output_config={"effort": "high"}, messages=[ {"role": "user", "content": "Find all N+1 queries in this 3,000-line Django module."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": previous_analysis}, # Step down without cache bust: {"role": "system", "content": [], "output_config": {"effort": "low"}}, {"role": "user", "content": "List the top three as one-line bullets."}, ], betas=["mid-conversation-output-config-2026-07-01"], ) ```
**The limits.** Only `claude-fable-5-1`, `claude-mythos-5-1`, and `claude-opus-5` support per-message effort; other models (including Fable 5 and Sonnet 4.6) return a 400. Use `client.beta.messages.create` — the standard path ignores the beta header. The system message must carry empty `content`; text in it triggers the normal mid-conversation placement rules and can fail validation. On Opus 5 at `xhigh` or `max` effort, thinking cannot be disabled — per-message effort cannot work around that constraint.
A GitHub issue documented that the older `/effort` slash command caused full cache misses on Opus 4.7 in 5 of 6 measured transitions. The per-message form was designed specifically to avoid that pattern on the newer models.
**Sources:** [Per-message effort (beta) — Anthropic Platform Docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort#change-effort-mid-conversation-beta) · [GitHub issue #61984: /effort changes cause cache misses on Opus 4.7 — anthropics/claude-code](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/61984) · [Claude effort control and mid-conversation system messages — AI for Anything](https://www.aiforanything.io/blog/claude-effort-control-mid-conversation-system-messages-api-guide-2026)

item.title: Your Claude Agents Weren't in Code Review. `ant apply` Changes That.
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: ant apply (ant CLI v1.30.0, Sep 3) declares Claude Platform resources — agents, skills, environments, memory stores, deployments — as files in your repo and reconciles them against the API with a plan-approve-apply loop.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: `ant apply` (ant CLI v1.30.0, released Sep 3) declares your Claude Platform agents, skills, environments, memory stores, and deployments as files in your repo — Terraform-style plan, approve, apply.**
Before this, your agent's system prompt and model config lived in a Console form or an ad-hoc API call that left no trace in git. `ant apply` treats them as code: you PR them, review them, and roll them back like everything else.
**The minimal workflow:**
Write your agent as a Markdown file — frontmatter is config, body is the system prompt:
```markdown # agents/summarizer.md --- name: Summarizer model: claude-opus-5 tools: - type: agent_toolset_20260401 --- You are a helpful assistant that writes concise summaries. ```
Run `ant apply agents/summarizer.md`. The CLI prints a plan, waits for approval, creates the resource, and writes `claude-lock.json`. Commit the lockfile — it maps each file to its API resource ID. The next run on any machine reads the lockfile and updates rather than duplicates.
**CI setup:**
```yaml # On PRs: print the plan, informational only (exits 0 even if blocked) - run: ant apply --dry-run .
# On merge: apply without prompting - run: ant apply --yes . - run: git add claude-lock.json && git commit -m "update claude-lock.json [skip ci]" ```
Resources refer to each other by file path. Your deployment YAML can name `../agents/reviewer.md`; `ant apply` resolves real API IDs at create time in dependency order. Skill references can be GitHub URLs pointing to a directory in any repo, pinned to a commit.
**Real limits:**
- **Can't adopt a resource you already built in the Console**: applying a file that describes an existing agent creates a second one. Use the Console's **Export as code** button to get a starting lockfile. - **Nothing serializes the lockfile in CI** — two concurrent `ant apply` runs will conflict. Serialize your CI jobs. - Requires ant CLI v1.30.0+; use [Workload Identity Federation](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/workload-identity-federation) for CI auth rather than a stored API key.
**Sources:** [`ant apply` docs — platform.claude.com](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/cli-sdks-libraries/cli/apply) · [Terraform-Style Workflow for Claude Agents — AlphaSignal](https://alphasignal.ai/news/anthropic-ships-terraform-style-workflow-to-deploy-claude-agents-from-code) · [Claude Developer Platform release notes (Sep 3) — platform.claude.com](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/release-notes/overview)

item.title: Four Chunking Strategies for RAG — and the Default That's Right 80% of the Time
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Most RAG pipelines default to fixed-size chunking — the lowest-recall strategy. Recursive character splitting at 400-512 tokens beats it in two lines; semantic chunking adds 9% recall at embedding cost.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: Most RAG pipelines use fixed-size chunking by default — lowest recall, easiest to swap. Recursive character splitting at 400–512 tokens beats it with two lines of code; semantic chunking adds recall but costs an embedding call per sentence.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** choose a chunking strategy for your document type, replace naive splitting with LangChain's `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter`, and know exactly when semantic chunking's accuracy gain is worth its compute cost.
Chunking controls what your retriever sees. A chunk that splits mid-sentence or folds three topics together embeds poorly, and poor embeddings lose recall before your reranker or LLM touches anything.
**The four strategies (fastest to most accurate):**
**1. Fixed-size (baseline).** Splits at a hard character or token limit. Fastest; fragments sentences mid-thought. Use for prototyping only.
**2. Recursive character (recommended default).** Splits at a hierarchy — `["\n\n", "\n", ". ", " ", ""]` — paragraph breaks first, then lines, then sentences — respecting natural boundaries without reading the content. A February 2026 benchmark by Vecta across 50 academic papers placed this first at 69% end-to-end accuracy, 85–90% retrieval recall:
```python from langchain.text_splitter import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter
splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter( chunk_size=512, # tokens chunk_overlap=50, # ~10% overlap preserves cross-chunk context separators=["\n\n", "\n", ". ", " ", ""] ) chunks = splitter.split_text(doc_text) ```
Start here for 80% of RAG workloads: 400–512 tokens, 10–20% overlap.
**3. Page-level (PDFs).** Each page is a chunk. Topped NVIDIA's 2024 retrieval benchmark (0.648 accuracy). Only applies to paginated documents where page boundaries carry meaning — financial reports, slide decks. Useless for long-form web content where pages are arbitrary.
**4. Semantic chunking.** Embed every sentence, split where cosine similarity between adjacent sentences drops — each chunk stays on one topic regardless of length. Adds up to 9% recall over recursive splitting, per a Vectara/NAACL 2025 study. The cost: one embedding API call per sentence at ingest time, which compounds on large corpora. Threshold also requires tuning per corpus.
**The decision rule:** start with recursive character splitting at 400–512 tokens + 50-token overlap. Move to semantic chunking only if evaluation shows retrieval quality is the bottleneck *and* you can afford the ingest embedding compute.
**Sources:** [Best Chunking Strategies for RAG (2026) — Firecrawl](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/best-chunking-strategies-rag) · [RAG Tutorial 2026 #8: Text Chunking Strategies — YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=POE8LDjdAw4) · [RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter — LangChain docs](https://python.langchain.com/docs/modules/data_connection/document_transformers/recursive_text_splitter/)

item.title: Claude Design Generates at One Viewport Width — Four Things to Check Before You Hand Off
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Design's canvas doesn't simulate responsive behavior. Four failure modes that survive a good prompt: fixed pixel widths, missing flex-wrap, hardcoded font sizes, and absolute-positioned elements.
item.content:encoded:
**Before you hand Claude Design output to Claude Code: four responsive failure modes that survive a good prompt, and the two-pass review that catches them before any code is written.**
Claude Design generates screens at a fixed canvas width. The artboards look complete — but responsive behavior isn't simulated in the canvas. There's no breakpoint preview, no flex-wrap test, no dynamic content check. What typically arrives in Claude Code's first pass:
1. **Fixed pixel widths** — `width: 800px` instead of `max-width` or a percentage 2. **Missing flex-wrap** — horizontal item rows that overflow on narrow viewports 3. **Hardcoded font sizes** — `font-size: 20px` where `clamp()` or a type scale belongs 4. **Absolutely positioned elements** that collide when the viewport narrows
**Two-pass review before you commit to the implementation:**
**Pass 1 — in Claude Design:** Ask "Check this screen for fixed widths, overflow risks, and anything that won't adapt to a narrower layout." Claude Design can flag most of these in text even though the canvas doesn't resize. If a component inventory is already in the session context, this also catches elements that drift between screens.
**Pass 2 — in the browser:** Once the exported bundle lands in your repo, resize to 375px and 768px before writing any new code. Add the breakpoints you need to the handoff message or your CLAUDE.md so Claude Code applies them from the first file it touches.
**The limit:** The canvas editor shows one artboard width and doesn't preview responsive states. Until Claude Design adds breakpoint views, browser testing is the only way to verify responsive behavior.
**Sources:** [From Prompt to Pull Request: Claude Design + Claude Code — DEV Community](https://dev.to/bilelsalemdev/from-prompt-to-pull-request-using-claude-design-claude-code-and-github-together-3m00) · [Claude Design responsive output — The Human Co.](https://thehumanco.org/ai-resources/claude-design-update-brand-consistency) · [The Claude Design Handoff Playbook — Hyperautomation Labs](https://hyperautomationlabs.co/free/claude-design-long)

item.title: Claude Code Hangs in CI Because It's Waiting for You — `--permission-prompts none` Fixes That
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Three settings for a fully unattended Claude Code run in CI: --permission-prompts none auto-denies unexpected prompts, an explicit allow list handles tool permissions, and bashOutputMaxChars keeps logs from being silently truncated.
item.content:encoded:
**`--permission-prompts none` + auto mode + `bashOutputMaxChars` gives you a Claude Code run that never hangs on a prompt and always surfaces the actual failure, not a timeout.**
A Claude Code agent running in CI hits a permission prompt for an action outside its allow list — and the job silently times out rather than failing. No error, no output, just a hung runner. Three settings together prevent this:
**1. `--permission-prompts none`** (v2.1.259)
Any action that would normally open a permission prompt is auto-denied instead:
```bash claude -p --permission-prompts none "run tests, fix any failures, commit the result" ```
This layers on top of whatever permission mode is active. Auto mode still runs its classifier; anything that falls through to a prompt gets denied rather than blocking the runner.
**2. An explicit allow list in `.claude/settings.json`**
Tell Claude exactly what it's trusted to do in this pipeline so safe actions pass auto mode without a classification delay:
```json { "permissions": { "allow": ["Bash(npm test)", "Bash(npm run lint)", "Edit"], "deny": ["Bash(git push)", "Bash(git commit)"] } } ```
**3. `bashOutputMaxChars`** (v2.1.261)
When a test log exceeds the default inline limit, Claude receives a file path instead of the actual errors. Raise the cap so the full output arrives:
```json { "bashOutputMaxChars": 65536 } ```
**The limit:** This combination keeps the run alive and gives Claude the information it needs — but you still need to review the diff before merging. With `--permission-prompts none`, Claude can't ask when it's unsure; ambiguous actions fail silently rather than being recovered.
**Sources:** [Claude Code auto mode — Anthropic docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/core-concepts/auto-mode) · [Running Claude Code agents in CI — Tembo.io](https://www.tembo.io/blog/claude-code-subagents) · [v2.1.259 changelog](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog)

item.title: Your RAG Retriever Pulls the Right Text — From Last Year's Policy Doc. Metadata Filters Fix That.
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Metadata filtering scopes vector search to documents matching hard attributes — category, year, tenant — before similarity scoring runs, so contextually wrong chunks never compete for top-k slots.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** scope your vector search by document attributes — category, date, tenant, access tier — so retrieval never surfaces semantically close text from the contextually wrong document.
Similarity search finds chunks that are close in embedding space. It doesn't know that "refund policy" from last year's version is the wrong document to surface today. Metadata filtering adds a hard constraint that runs inside the vector index, before similarity scoring starts — only matching chunks enter the retrieval pool.
**At ingest, store structured payload fields alongside your embedding:**
```python from qdrant_client import QdrantClient, models
client = QdrantClient("localhost", port=6333)
client.upsert( collection_name="docs", points=[models.PointStruct( id=chunk_id, vector=embedding, payload={"category": "policy", "year": 2026, "department": "support"} )] ) ```
**At query time, add a filter before similarity scoring runs:**
```python from qdrant_client.http.models import Filter, FieldCondition, MatchValue
results = client.search( collection_name="docs", query_vector=query_embedding, query_filter=Filter(must=[ FieldCondition(key="category", match=MatchValue(value="policy")), FieldCondition(key="year", match=MatchValue(value=2026)) ]), limit=5 ) ```
**Index every field you filter on — without this, filtered queries fall back to a full scan:**
```python client.create_payload_index("docs", "category", field_schema="keyword") client.create_payload_index("docs", "year", field_schema="integer") ```
Chroma uses `where={"year": 2026}`. Pinecone uses a `filter` dict. LangChain's `SelfQueryRetriever` can auto-generate the filter object from a natural language question — useful when users write free-text queries that carry implicit filter intent ("show me last year's support tickets").
**The real limit:** filtering only helps if the metadata is stored at ingest time. Retroactively adding category labels to thousands of existing chunks is the hard part, not the query syntax.
**Sources:** [RAG #8: Metadata Filtering in Vector Databases Explained — YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bBFu6fbmPDk) · [Qdrant filtering docs](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/concepts/filtering/) · [Filter RAG Search Results with Document Metadata Tags — Markaicode](https://markaicode.com/rag-metadata-filtering-document-tags/)

item.title: The Names You Give Design Elements in Claude Design Are What Claude Code Uses to Look Up Components
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Design generates screens with generic element names. Rename them to your actual component names before exporting — Claude Code uses those names to look up your real components.
item.content:encoded:
**Claude Design generates screens with generic element names like "Card" and "Button." Before you export, rename every element to the actual name from your component library — Claude Code uses those names to find your real components, not build new ones.**
When Claude Design generates a screen, its layer panel fills up with generic names: "Card," "Input Field," "Modal Overlay." Those names look reasonable, but they're not your component names. When Claude Code sees the exported design and tries to implement it, it searches your codebase for a component called "Card" — and if your actual component is `<ProductCard>` or `<DashboardCard>`, it won't find it. It builds a fallback from scratch instead.
**The naming pass** happens before you export, in Claude Design's layer panel:
``` Prompt: "List every element on this screen as a flat list with its current name. I'll rename them." ```
Go through the list and rename each element to its actual component name from your library. For a design system with a `<DataTable>`, rename "Table" → "DataTable." For `<PrimaryButton>`, rename "Button" → "PrimaryButton." Keep the exact casing your codebase uses.
**Base components** (Button, TextField, Checkbox) can keep their generic name if that's what your library calls them. The rename only matters where your library diverges from the generic.
**Add a component map to DESIGN.md** so Claude Code knows which design element names map to which components:
```md ## Component name map | Design element | Component | |---|---| | ProductCard | `<ProductCard variant="summary" />` | | HeroSection | `<PageHero />` | | FilterDrawer | `<SidebarFilter />` | ```
**Worst failure mode:** modals. A generic "Modal Overlay" becomes a bespoke div with manually managed z-index and focus trapping, bypassing whatever modal system you already have. If your library has `<DialogModal>` or `<Sheet>`, name it that in the design panel.
**One limit:** this only helps when your library uses descriptive names. If your components are named by role (Button, Input) rather than by design intent (PrimaryAction, SearchInput), Claude Code's component lookup lands on the right component regardless — the naming pass matters most for divergent vocabularies.
**Sources:** [claudelab.net — pre-handoff component naming](https://claudelab.net/workflow/component-naming-handoff/) · [aakashg/claude-design-pm-toolkit](https://github.com/aakashg/claude-design-pm-toolkit) · [dev.to/bilelsalemdev — naming components in Claude Design](https://dev.to/bilelsalemdev/naming-components-claude-design-before-handoff)

item.title: Your Fable 5.1 Agent Returns a 400 When You Edit Earlier Turns — Here's the Fix
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Fable 5.1 validates thinking-block provenance for accounts after August 31 — any harness that edits earlier turns mid-session returns a 400. Use turn-scoped system messages instead.
item.content:encoded:
**Fable 5.1 validates thinking-block provenance. For accounts created after August 31, any harness that edits an earlier turn mid-session gets a 400: "bound to a different conversation." The fix is turn-scoped system messages — not edited history.**
The error surfaces in agentic setups: a harness that injects context by rewriting an earlier turn, or that swaps tool definitions mid-session, now gets back:
``` 400 Bad Request thinking_block_binding: bound to a different conversation ```
**What triggers it:** - Editing any turn earlier than the current one mid-session - Changing the tool list between turns in the same session - Client-side in-place summarization that rewrites earlier assistant turns
**The fix — turn-scoped system messages.** Instead of editing history, inject context as a system message scoped to clear after the next user turn:
```json { "role": "system", "content": "...", "clear_at": "next_user_message" } ```
Requires beta header: `anthropic-beta: mid-conversation-system-clear-at-2026-08-21`.
**Tool changes** must happen between sessions (after the conversation ends), not mid-session. If you need a different tool set for a sub-task, start a fresh session.
**Whole-history compaction** is still valid — collapse all prior turns into a single summary turn and start fresh. That resets provenance cleanly. The harness pattern to avoid is surgical rewriting of individual earlier turns.
**Detection:** The beta header `anthropic-beta: thinking-binding-controls-2026-08-01` exposes `thinking.block_binding.prefix_mismatch_behavior`. Set it to `"drop_block"` to downgrade the error to a warning (thinking blocks from mismatched history are silently dropped) while you migrate your harness.
**One limit:** enforcement is currently scoped to accounts created after August 31, 2026. Earlier accounts see the old behavior until future model versions extend enforcement universally — migrate now rather than after the cutover.
**Sources:** [Anthropic Fable 5.1 guide](https://www.anthropic.com/research/fable-51-guide) · [AI Unfiltered — Fable 5.1 turn editing](https://arturmarkus.com/ai-unfiltered/fable-51-turn-editing/) · [Anthropic preserved-thinking docs](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/extended-thinking/preserved-thinking)

item.content:encoded:
**Two items developers need to know about this weekend: Nvidia is buying HuggingFace for $12.93B — a hardware company will own the primary open-model hub — and Claude Code's temporary +50% limits end September 14, which means an effective 17% cut from today's limits.**
**Nvidia acquires HuggingFace — $12.93B, closes H1 2027**
Announced September 3. Nvidia is paying $12.93B for HuggingFace, the host of 3M+ models, 500K datasets, and 18M developers. Jensen Huang's stated position: maintain the open-ecosystem mission, no vendor lock-in. The obvious concern from the Forrester analysis: Nvidia has every incentive to optimize HuggingFace tooling for CUDA hardware, and the pressure to do so will grow as the deal ages.
For engineers who depend on HuggingFace for model access, dataset pipelines, or the Hub API: the platform keeps running under existing terms through close. Post-close behavior depends on what "open ecosystem" means in practice once quarterly earnings expectations apply.
The harder question is what this does to the trust stack under open-weights models. HuggingFace has been a neutral host. Nvidia is not.
**Claude Code limits drop 17% on September 14**
In May, Anthropic added a temporary +50% boost to Claude Code's per-session and daily limits (the SpaceX compute partnership announcement). That boost ends September 14. The permanent increase from May — +25% above the pre-May baseline — stays. Net result: limits drop from the current boosted level to the permanent floor, which is 17% below where they are today.
Session limits are unaffected. The change hits the daily and per-period aggregate caps.
If you're doing large refactors or multi-day agentic runs scheduled around current limits, plan for the reduction now rather than hitting it mid-task on the 14th.

item.title: Your Claude Code Context Is Burning on Skills You Never Use. /skill-doctor Shows the Bill.
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code v2.1.261 adds /skill-doctor (shows unused skills and their context cost per turn) and bashOutputMaxChars/taskOutputMaxChars settings (raise inline output cap to 128K to fix truncated logs).
item.content:encoded:
**Every skill loaded from CLAUDE.md burns tokens every turn whether it helped or not — v2.1.261 adds a diagnostic that shows exactly which ones to cut, and a setting that stops build logs from being silently truncated.**
Every skill listed in auto-load burns context tokens on every turn — whether it fires or not. If your session pulls in a dozen skills, most of them are probably dead weight. Run the new diagnostic:
``` /skill-doctor ```
The command prints a table: skill name, used or unused in this session, and its approximate context cost per turn. Drop the unused ones, or move rarely-needed skills out of global auto-load and into project-specific settings so they only load when they're relevant.
The second fix is for engineers who hit silently truncated command output. When a build log or test run exceeds Claude's default inline limit, the output gets offloaded to a file — Claude reads a filename, not the actual errors. Raise the cap in `.claude/settings.json`:
```json { "bashOutputMaxChars": 65536, "taskOutputMaxChars": 65536 } ```
The maximum is 128K characters. Match it to your actual worst-case output — a full `jest --verbose` run, a `cargo build` log — and don't go higher than you need. Every command above your old cap now sends its output inline, which means Claude sees the real failure instead of a file path, but also means context cost goes up proportionally on large outputs.
One more addition in v2.1.261: `--append-subagent-system-prompt-file <path>` reads a subagent system prompt from a file — useful when the prompt is too long to pass as a command-line argument.
One limit: raising `bashOutputMaxChars` to 128K is not free — it moves 128K of characters into context on every large command, whether Claude needed to read all of it or not. Set it to what your actual failure output requires; running at the ceiling when your logs are 20K wastes context on every tool call.
**Sources:** [Claude Code changelog](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog) · [AI/TLDR — Claude Code 2.1.261](https://ai-tldr.dev/releases/anthropic-claude-code-2-1-261/)

item.title: GPT-6 Astra Opens to API: What the Pricing Means for Engineers Who Route Across Models
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: GPT-6 Astra's public rollout begins today — at $10/$50/M tokens per OpenAI's stated rates, it's 3-4x the cost of current workhorse models, which defines where it fits in a multi-provider stack.
item.content:encoded:
**GPT-6 Astra begins its public API rollout today. Per OpenAI's stated rates: $10/$50 per million tokens — 3–4× the cost of Claude Sonnet 5 or GPT-4o — which narrows where it fits in a cost-conscious multi-provider stack.**
GPT-6 Astra's limited-partner preview started September 3. Public rollout to Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users begins today; API access follows in the coming days. Per OpenAI's stated pricing: $10/M input, $50/M output, $1/M for cached input. Batch and flex processing at half price; Fast mode at 2×. Context window: 1,050,000 tokens; max output: 128K tokens.
The technical distinction: a "recurrent depth" reasoning technique that OpenAI says improves focus and multi-step task handling. Researchers have flagged this design as less transparent than standard chain-of-thought — internal reasoning steps are obscured, making the model harder to audit or steer.
For a multi-provider routing setup: Astra's cost profile places it firmly in the premium tier — useful for hard reasoning, large-document work, and complex multi-step agents where accuracy matters more than throughput cost. At 3–4× the rate of current workhorse models (per OpenAI's and Anthropic's respective published pricing), it's not a replacement for Claude Sonnet 5 or GPT-4o on routine calls.
